key_facts: Demand is the ability and willingness to buy specific quantities of a good at alternative prices in a given time period, ceteris paribus.
Supply is the ability and willingness to sell (produce) specific quantities of a good at alternative prices in a given time period, ceteris paribus.
The law of demand states that the quantity of a good demanded in a given time period increases as its price falls, ceteris paribus.

The determinants of demand include: tastes (desire for this and other goods), income of the consumer, other goods (their availability and price), expectations (for income/prices/tastes), and the number of buyers.
A 'change in quantity demanded' refers to movements along a given demand curve in response to price changes of the good itself - distinct from a 'change in demand' which shifts the entire curve.
generated_text: Introduction: The Two Sides of a Market Every market transaction has two fundamental sides: supply and demand . These two forces interact to determine the prices we pay and the quantities of goods and services that are bought and sold. Understanding how they work is the foundation of microeconomics. Understanding Demand What is Demand? Demand is defined as the ability and willingness to buy specific quantities of a good at alternative prices in a given time period, assuming all other factors are held constant (a condition known as ceteris paribus ). Quantity Demanded refers to the specific amount of a good that buyers are willing and able to purchase at a single, specific price. The Law of Demand The law of demand is a fundamental principle stating that, ceteris paribus , the quantity of a good demanded in a given time period increases as its price falls. In simpler terms, people tend to buy more of something when it becomes cheaper. The Demand Curve This inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded is visualized by the demand curve, which slopes downward from left to right. It graphically shows that as the price (P) on the vertical axis decreases, the quantity demanded (Qd) on the horizontal axis increases. Change in Quantity Demanded vs. Change in Demand It is crucial to distinguish between two types of changes related to demand: Change in Quantity Demanded: This is a movement along a given demand curve. It is caused only by a change in the price of the good itself. For example, if the price of a coffee drops from $4 to $3, consumers move down along the existing demand curve to a point with a higher quantity demanded. Change in Demand: This is a shift of the entire demand curve, either to the left (a decrease in demand) or to the right (an increase in demand). This shift is caused by a change in a non-price factor. Determinants of Demand (Demand Shifters) The non-price factors that can shift the entire demand curve are known as the determinants of demand. They include: Tastes: Changes in consumer preferences or desire for a good. Income: A change in consumers' income. For a normal good , higher income increases demand. For an inferior good , higher income decreases demand. Other Goods: The availability and price of related goods, such as substitutes and complements. Expectations: Consumers' expectations about their future income, future prices, or tastes. Number of Buyers: An increase or decrease in the number of consumers in the market. Understanding Supply What is Supply? Supply is the ability and willingness to sell (or produce) specific quantities of a good at alternative prices in a given time period, ceteris paribus . It is an expression of sellers' intentions, not necessarily a statement of actual sales. The Law of Supply The law of supply states that, ceteris paribus , the quantity of a good supplied in a given time period increases as its price increases. Producers are willing to offer larger quantities for sale at higher prices because it is more profitable. The Supply Curve The supply curve illustrates this direct relationship, sloping upward from left to right. As the price (P) increases, the quantity supplied (Qs) also increases. Change in Quantity Supplied vs. Change in Supply Similar to demand, we must distinguish between: Change in Quantity Supplied: A movement along the supply curve caused by a change in the good's own price. Change in Supply: A shift of the entire supply curve to the right (an increase in supply) or to the left (a decrease in supply). This is caused by a change in a non-price determinant. Determinants of Supply (Supply Shifters) Factors that can shift the supply curve include: Input Prices: The costs of resources used to produce the good. An increase in input prices (like wages or raw materials) will likely decrease supply. Technology: Advancements in production technology can reduce costs and increase supply. Expectations: Sellers' expectations about future prices. Number of Sellers: An increase or decrease in the number of producers in the market. Market Equilibrium: Where Supply Meets Demand Finding Equilibrium The market reaches equilibrium at the point where the supply and demand curves intersect. At this point, a balance is achieved: The Equilibrium Price is the price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded. The Equilibrium Quantity is the quantity supplied and demanded at that equilibrium price. At equilibrium, the market is said to "clear," and there is no pressure for the price to rise or fall. Markets Out of Equilibrium When the market price is not at equilibrium, either a surplus or a shortage will occur, creating pressure for the price to change. Surplus (Excess Supply): If the price is set above the equilibrium price, the quantity supplied will be greater than the quantity demanded. To sell their excess inventory, sellers will cut prices, pushing the market back toward equilibrium. Shortage (Excess Demand): If the price is set below the equilibrium price, the quantity demanded will be greater than the quantity supplied. With too many buyers chasing too few goods, the price will be bid up, moving the market back toward equilibrium. Analyzing Changes in Equilibrium When a non-price determinant changes, a curve shifts, leading to a new equilibrium. Consider the market for hybrid cars: Event: An increase in the price of gas. This makes hybrids more desirable, shifting the demand curve to the right. The result is a higher equilibrium price and quantity for hybrid cars. Event: New technology reduces production costs. This makes producing hybrids more profitable, shifting the supply curve to the right. The result is a lower equilibrium price and a higher equilibrium quantity. Events: Both happen at once. If demand shifts right and supply also shifts right, the equilibrium quantity will definitely increase. However, the effect on the equilibrium price is ambiguous; it depends on the relative size of the shifts in demand and supply. The Impact of Government Policies Governments sometimes intervene in markets through price controls or taxes, which can alter market outcomes. Price Ceilings A price ceiling is a legal maximum on the price at which a good can be sold. If the ceiling is set above the equilibrium price, it is not binding and has no effect on the market. If the ceiling is set below the equilibrium price, it is binding and creates a shortage , because quantity demanded will exceed quantity supplied. Price Floors A price floor is a legal minimum on the price at which a good can be sold. The minimum wage is a common example. If the floor is set below the equilibrium price, it is not binding . If the floor is set above the equilibrium price, it is binding and creates a surplus , because quantity supplied will exceed quantity demanded. Taxes When the government imposes a tax on a good, it creates a wedge between the price buyers pay (PB) and the price sellers receive (PS). This reduces the equilibrium quantity traded. A tax on sellers shifts the supply curve upward (to the left). A tax on buyers shifts the demand curve downward (to the left). The final outcome—the new quantity, the price buyers pay, and the price sellers receive—is the same regardless of whether the tax is levied on buyers or sellers. Summary This lesson covered the core model of supply and demand. Key takeaways include: The Law of Demand states that price and quantity demanded are inversely related. The Law of Supply states that price and quantity supplied are directly related. Market equilibrium occurs at the price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded, clearing the market. A change in a good's own price causes a movement along its respective curve, while a change in a non-price determinant causes a shift of the entire curve. Government interventions like binding price ceilings can cause shortages, binding price floors can cause surpluses, and taxes reduce the quantity traded and create a wedge between the price paid by buyers and received by sellers.
